# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

- session-start-hook: Creating and developing startup hooks for Claude Code on the web. Use when the user wants to set up a repository for Claude Code on the web, create a SessionStart hook to ensure their project can run tests and linters during web sessions.
- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- bump-version: Raise the project's version — a minor bump by default. Use when the owner says "bump version".
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).

First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch
- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. 19	// code before acting (DESIGN §7).
20	
21	export const DEFAULT_ENDPOINT = 'default';
22	
23	// The endpoint is a ROUTINE'S API TRIGGER — `POST /v1/claude_code/routines/
24	// <trigger-id>/fire` with a per-routine bearer token — which is what Claude Code
25	// on the web actually exposes to an HTTP caller. Three consequences the design's
26	// "a CCR API call" did not spell out, each verified against the routines docs
27	// rather than assumed:
28	//
29	//  - THE BEHAVIOR IS THE ROUTINE'S STORED PROMPT, not ours. `text` reaches the
30	//    session wrapped in a `<routine-fire-payload>` block explicitly labelled
31	//    untrusted, and a routine acts on it only because its own saved prompt says
32	//    to. That is the issue-is-data posture arriving for free at one more hop: our
33	//    payload names an item, and every instruction comes from a stored artifact.
34	//    The routine's stored prompt is one line pointing at `instructions.md` beside
35	//    this file, so the whole of what a session does is tracked and reviewed.
36	//  - THE BODY CARRIES ONE FIELD. `text` is freeform and unparsed — structured
37	//    JSON would arrive as a literal string — so the item number and nonce go in
38	//    as prose, and nothing else goes in at all.
39	//  - THERE IS NO IDEMPOTENCY KEY (standing entry 11, answered: the endpoint
40	//    offers none), which is exactly why THIS MODULE CALLS ONCE PER ITEM AND NEVER
41	//    RETRIES. A retry is only safe when you know the first call did nothing, and
42	//    a client-side timeout is the one case where you cannot know — the session
43	//    may well have started. Retrying there is what would make invocation
44	//    at-least-once and put two sessions on one item; declining to retry is what
45	//    keeps it at-most-once and lets the whole agent-side claim protocol delete.
46	//    An outcome we did not learn is reported as UNKNOWN and resolved by the agent
47	//    leash, which is a rule that already exists, rather than by a guess here.
48	//
49	// The beta header is dated and the endpoint is a research preview whose two most
50	// recent header versions keep working, so it lives in config with a default here
51	// — a rotation is then a config edit on one repo, never an engine release the
52	// whole fleet waits for.
53	export const DEFAULT_HEADERS = Object.freeze({
54	  'anthropic-beta': 'experimental-cc-routine-2026-04-01',
55	  'anthropic-version': '2023-06-01',
56	});
57	
58	// The endpoint a task's hand-off calls, resolved against the repo's config.
59	// Returns `{ name, url, tokenEnv, headers }` or `{ name, error }` — a task naming
60	// an endpoint the repo has not configured is a repo-configuration fact, reported
61	// where the operator reads it, never a crash.
62	export function resolveEndpoint(config, task) {
63	  const name = task?.decl?.invocation_endpoint ?? DEFAULT_ENDPOINT;
64	  const endpoints = config?.taskScheduler?.endpoints ?? {};
65	  const entry = endpoints[name];
66	  if (!entry) {
67	    return { name, error: `this repo's config declares no invocation endpoint "${name}" (taskScheduler.endpoints)` };
68	  }
69	  if (!entry.url) return { name, error: `invocation endpoint "${name}" declares no url` };
70	  if (!entry.tokenSecret) return { name, error: `invocation endpoint "${name}" declares no tokenSecret (the NAME of the repo Actions secret holding its token)` };
71	  return { name, url: entry.url, tokenEnv: entry.tokenSecret, headers: { ...DEFAULT_HEADERS, ...(entry.headers ?? {}) } };
72	}
73	
74	// The fire payload: which item, and the nonce that proves this call is the one
75	// the hand-off comment recorded. Prose, not JSON — the field is freeform and
76	// unparsed, so a structured payload would arrive as a literal string — and
77	// deliberately free of instructions, because the routine's stored prompt is what
78	// says how to act on it (see `instructions.md`). The session still validates
79	// the item in code before touching it: a payload labelled untrusted is trusted no
80	// more than a label event was.
81	export const firePayload = ({ repo, item, nonce }) =>
82	  `Claudinite work item: ${repo}#${item.number}. Invocation nonce: ${nonce}.`;
83	
84	// The invoker seam the executor calls, exactly once per item. Failure is DATA,
85	// never a throw, and it comes in two kinds the caller must treat differently:
86	//
87	//   { ok: true, sessionId, sessionUrl }   the routine fired; a session exists
88	//   { ok: false, answered: true, error }  the endpoint ANSWERED and refused —
89	//                                         no session, and the cause is a
90	//                                         configuration fault a retry cannot fix
91	//   { ok: false, answered: false, error } no answer reached us — a timeout, a
92	//                                         dropped connection. The session may or
93	//                                         may not exist, and nothing here may
94	//                                         guess which.
95	export function agentInvoker({ repo, config, env = process.env, fetchImpl = fetch, timeoutMs = 60e3 }) {
96	  return async function invoke({ task, item, nonce }) {
97	    const endpoint = resolveEndpoint(config, task);
98	    // A configuration fault, decided before any call: definite, and no session.
99	    if (endpoint.error) return { ok: false, answered: true, error: endpoint.error };
100	    const token = env[endpoint.tokenEnv];
101	    if (!token) {
102	      // The `required_secrets` posture, applied to the endpoint token: nothing
103	      // fails silently, the task just doesn't work yet, and the item names which
104	      // secret to set (DESIGN §14.7).
105	      return { ok: false, answered: true, error: `the Actions secret \`${endpoint.tokenEnv}\` for invocation endpoint "${endpoint.name}" is not set in this repo` };
106	    }
107	
108	    const payload = { text: firePayload({ repo, item, nonce }) };
109	
110	    // ONE call. No loop, and deliberately no `attempts` knob for anyone to raise.
111	    try {
112	      const res = await fetchImpl(endpoint.url, {
113	        method: 'POST',
114	        headers: {
115	          ...endpoint.headers,
116	          'content-type': 'application/json',
117	          authorization: `Bearer ${token}`,
118	          'user-agent': 'claudinite-executor',
119	        },
120	        body: JSON.stringify(payload),
121	        signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs),
122	      });
123	      let json = null;
124	      try { json = await res.json(); } catch { json = null; }
125	      if (res.status >= 200 && res.status < 300) {
126	        return {
127	          ok: true,
128	          sessionId: json?.claude_code_session_id ?? null,
129	          sessionUrl: json?.claude_code_session_url ?? null,
130	        };
131	      }
132	      // A status came back, so the endpoint decided: no session was started, and
133	      // the cause is a token, a URL or a routine — none of which a retry fixes.
134	      return {
135	        ok: false, answered: true,
136	        error: `endpoint "${endpoint.name}" returned ${res.status}${json?.error ? `: ${JSON.stringify(json.error)}` : ''}`,
137	      };
138	    } catch (e) {
139	      // Nothing came back. The request may have landed and started a session, so
140	      // this is the one outcome that must never be retried and never be reported
141	      // as a failure — it is genuinely unknown, and the caller says so on the item.
142	      return { ok: false, answered: false, error: `endpoint "${endpoint.name}" gave no answer: ${e.message}` };
143	    }
144	  };
145	}

# tidy-branches worker

The **assess-only** branch third of the repo tidy-up: a weekly pass over the repo's open branches — run
only when a branch was actually created or pushed in the window — then record the picture. You run under
the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue; its **Context section is binding scope** — it lists
the branches to assess. Work only those; don't enumerate the repo yourself. GitHub access is **MCP-only**
(`mcp__github__*`).

The task's declared outcome ceiling is **`none`**, and this dimension is read-only besides: **never delete,
push, or merge a branch**, and never open or merge a PR. You recommend; a human acts. The only thing you
write is this task's own tracker issue.

**Never assess the repo's own default branch.** The Context already excludes the known infra branches (the
orphan `conversation-logs` log stream and the `claudinite/maintenance` delivery branch) and the conventional
default names, but a precondition cannot look up the real default branch by name — that exclusion is your
responsibility here.

## 1. Assess each branch

For each branch in the Context list, run the
[single-branch-status](../../skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md) skill for its verdict — judged by
**content**, never the ref's auto-generated name. Collect:

- one line each for the branches carrying **genuine unmerged work** (`` `branch` — what it carries``);
- the rest collapsed into one `Safe to delete: N — a, b, c` line;
- any **orphaned** branch flagged for a human.

## 2. Reconcile this task's tracker

One standing tracker issue per repo, titled exactly `Claudinite tracker: Tidy Branches` — found by that
**exact title, never a fuzzy match**; create it **already closed** if absent (never a fresh issue per run,
never a bare number that can dangle). Each dimension keeps its **own** tracker, so three tasks never race
to rewrite one body.

Touch it two ways each run:

- **Rewrite the issue body** to today's **dated** snapshot: the branches carrying genuine unmerged work, the
  safe-to-delete count and names, and anything orphaned. The body is the live picture — it replaces last
  week's, it doesn't accumulate.
- **Add a dated comment** with today's status, so the body's snapshots leave a per-run trail.

Keep both short. **Never open, close, or reopen the tracker** — its state carries no meaning. The tracker
only *records* the recommendations; nothing here touches a branch.

`model: sonnet` — superseded / orphaned are judgment calls; the reconcile is mechanical aggregation.

1	// tidy-repo task: tidy-branches — the read-only branch third of the tidy sweep
2	// (per-project-scheduling DESIGN §6). One weekly full sweep over the repo's open
3	// branches: which carry genuine unmerged work, which are safe to delete. Recommends;
4	// never deletes. Worker: task.md. Issues and PRs are separate tasks — one dimension
5	// per task, each with its own trigger, scope, and tracker, so there is no ordering
6	// barrier.
7	//
8	// WEEKLY, and full every time it runs — but it only runs when a branch actually
9	// MOVED in the window. Branch cruft accumulates on a weekly clock, not a daily one,
10	// and the verdict is a standing recommendation for a human rather than a same-day
11	// alert, so the full sweep is a frequency DECLARATION, never a gate trick inside a
12	// daily task (DESIGN §3). What the sweep is NOT is unconditional: re-deriving the
13	// same verdicts over an unchanged pile of branches costs an agent run and produces a
14	// tracker rewrite identical to last week's. Scope stays full because a verdict is
15	// relative to the others (superseded-by, already-in-main); the GATE is newness.
16	//
17	// Self-contained (imports nothing): the whole contract is this default export.
18	
19	// Branches the tidy review must never assess. Beyond the default branch, the orphan
20	// `conversation-logs` branch is a grow_with_claudinite artifact (the captured-transcript
21	// stream, not project work) — it shares no history with main, so single-branch-status
22	// would flag it "orphaned" for a human on every run. It is infrastructure the tidy
23	// sweep ignores altogether. Kept as a bare literal, not an import: the pack-independence
24	// barrier forbids tidy-repo from reaching into grow_with_claudinite, and the name is a
25	// fixed, well-known one. The stable maintenance branch is likewise never a tidy target —
26	// it is Claudinite's own standing delivery branch, not project work.
27	const IGNORED_BRANCHES = new Set(['conversation-logs', 'claudinite/maintenance']);
28	
29	// A precondition has no repo handle, so it cannot look up the actual default branch
30	// name to drop it from the candidate set — and the `branches` signal carries every
31	// open branch, the default included. Presuming the conventional default names here
32	// keeps a repo whose only branch is its default from firing this task at all, which is
33	// the whole point of the gate. The worker (task.md) remains the authority that never
34	// assesses the repo's real default branch, so a repo whose default is unconventionally
35	// named is still safe — its default just also becomes a (cheap, read-only) candidate.
36	const PRESUMED_DEFAULT = new Set(['main', 'master']);
37	
38	export default {
39	  id: 'tidy-branches',
40	  frequency: 'weekly',                      // the weekly anchor (DESIGN §2); the full sweep is the declaration
41	  precondition_signals: ['branches'],       // names for the scope, `touched` for the gate
42	  agent_model: 'sonnet',                    // superseded / orphaned / already-in-main are judgment calls on content
43	  expected_outcome: 'none',                 // assess-only: never deletes, pushes, or merges; writes only its tracker
44	  agent_instructions: 'task.md',
45	  agent_execution_timeout: 600,             // one cheap diff-and-merge-base read per branch
46	
47	  // Two gates, in order. Is there a branch worth assessing at all — a repo carrying
48	  // nothing but its default branch (and the infra branches) stays silent. Then: did
49	  // any of them MOVE in the window. An unchanged set of branches yields the same
50	  // verdicts it yielded last run, so re-deriving them buys nothing; the standing
51	  // picture already lives in the tracker. When something did move, scope is still
52	  // the FULL set — a branch's verdict is relative to the others (superseded-by,
53	  // already-in-main), so assessing the new one alone would be assessing it blind.
54	  precondition(signals) {
55	    const assessable = (b) => !IGNORED_BRANCHES.has(b) && !PRESUMED_DEFAULT.has(b);
56	    const branches = (signals.branches?.names ?? []).filter(assessable);
57	    if (!branches.length) return { run: false, reason: 'no branches to assess beyond the default and the infra branches' };
58	
59	    const moved = (signals.branches?.touched ?? []).filter(assessable);
60	    if (!moved.length) {
61	      return { run: false, reason: `no branch created or moved in the window — the standing picture over ${branches.length} branch(es) is unchanged` };
62	    }
63	
64	    return {
65	      run: true,
66	      reason: `${moved.length} branch(es) moved in the window — full sweep over ${branches.length} branch(es)`,
67	      context: [`Branches to assess (read-only — recommend deletions, never delete): ${branches.join(', ')}.`],
68	    };
69	  },
70	};
71

The browser-speech pack's endpointing section carried a rule that was
always mechanically testable but had only ever been prose: interim
recognition results are the "user is still speaking" signal and are
never delivered to the caller as a transcript.

The static signature is sharp. An interim result is a revisable
hypothesis that looks exactly like a final one — same shape, same
transcript, same confidence, no error — and `isFinal` is the only thing
in the API that tells them apart. So a file that turns interim results
on AND handles the `result` event, but never reads `isFinal`, is
necessarily handing hypotheses to its caller: it acts on "heart" while
the user is still saying "heartland", and nothing throws, because the
code received a perfectly valid result and did something with it.

New check `stt-interim-results-gated` (blocking) asks exactly that
question, file-scoped in the style of `mic-capture-released`. Both
halves are required before it judges anything, which is what keeps it
quiet on the shapes that are not violations: a settings module that only
sets the flag has no handler to gate, and a recognizer with interim
results off gets no finals-vs-interim problem at all (engines omit
`isFinal` in that mode, so demanding it there would be noise). It reads
both DOM wiring forms, strips comments first, and treats the value token
of the assignment explicitly rather than with a lookahead — a lookahead
glued to `\s*` backtracks the whitespace to zero width and passes on the
`false` it was meant to reject, which is how the red run caught it.

Fixtures first, seen red against a no-op stub: three violating sources
(property wiring, addEventListener wiring, options-object form) all went
uncaught, while the seven clean ones already passed. The rule is also
held to the real extension/src tree, where stt-port.js gates on
`isFinal !== false` and is clean.

The prose stays whole. The deletion test says a paragraph goes only when
the check covers everything it describes, and this one's main remedy —
a pause monitor that discards the half-heard input and reopens a fresh
cycle — is not something the check enforces. Added the check pointer
beside it, in the convention the mic-release and mic-constraints
sections already use, and corrected the header's rule count.

npm run verify green (413 tests + requirement trace).

{"sha":"d773063faf5c718d8483fc67dc0f8809a265cb23","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/CrosswordChat/commit/d773063faf5c718d8483fc67dc0f8809a265cb23","commit":{"message":"browser-speech: convert the interim-results rule to a check (#134)

RULES.md's endpointing paragraph carried a clause no check enforced:
interim results are the "still speaking" signal only, "never delivered
to the caller". With `interimResults` on, the engine fires `result` for
every running hypothesis and `isFinal` is the only thing in the Web
Speech API that tells a hypothesis from an utterance — so a handler that
reads `.transcript` without it delivers the first partial guess as the
user's words. Nothing throws (the fragment is a well-formed transcript);
the user just gets the "heart heart" repeat bug.

New blocking rule `stt-interim-results-gated`, registered in pack.mjs.
It judges only files holding all three halves of the shape — interims
enabled (property or object-literal form, `false` excluded), `result`
wired (either DOM form), and a `transcript` read — then requires
`isFinal`. A config module that only flips the flag, a handler that only
receives, and `interimResults = false` are all quiet on purpose.

Six red-first fixtures in pack.test.mjs, proven in both directions:
neutering `run()` fails the two firing cases; removing the `isFinal`
guard and the `false` exclusion fails the two quiet cases and the real
extension/src/ scan.

Deletion test: the endpointing paragraph STAYS whole. The check covers
only its last clause — the pause monitor that discards and reopens, and
the measured 1.2 s / 1.8 s window, are judgment the check cannot make.
Per the skill, prose a check only partly covers is never trimmed; it
gets a pointer to the check instead. Prose edits are limited to that
pointer, the header's "five checks" count, and the README tables.

{"sha":"5c4dff1f08c0497b53909f6f0a8f0bf26c6c2e30","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/CrosswordChat/commit/5c4dff1f08c0497b53909f6f0a8f0bf26c6c2e30","commit":{"message":"Claudinite growth: convert the interim-results gating rule to a check

browser-speech's RULES.md has carried "interim results used only as the
'still speaking' signal, never delivered to the caller" as prose since the
pack was written. It is always-testable: `interimResults = true` changes what
`onresult` means, and `isFinal` is the only thing in the event that separates
a running hypothesis from the transcript — a static signature a scan can see.

New blocking check `stt-interim-results-gated` fires when a file enables
interim results and spells out its own result handler without ever consulting
`isFinal`. It reads the assignment's value (so an explicit `interimResults =
false` cannot fire) and requires the handler to be inline (so a delegated
`rec.onresult = this.handleResult`, whose gating lives in code the check
cannot see, is answered with silence rather than a guess).

Red-first, in both directions: the four firing fixtures fail with the rule
neutered, and the three quiet fixtures all wrongly fire against the naive
"says interimResults, never says isFinal" grep the scoping exists to avoid.
The rule is also clean on this repo's real extension/src tree.

Deletion test: the endpointing paragraph stays whole. The check covers only
its last clause; the paragraph also carries the pause-monitor remedy and the
measured 1.2 s / 1.8 s window, neither of which the check enforces — so it is
not redundant and is not trimmed. The pack's README and RULES.md check-count
map are updated to say the interim-delivery half is now mechanized.

{"sha":"9a1ca245910bb45c66208c69111dfb01aea50745","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/CrosswordChat/commit/9a1ca245910bb45c66208c69111dfb01aea50745","commit":{"message":"Add local pack voice-dialog: the language layer of a spoken interface

The repo's two local packs bound this territory without owning it:
browser-speech owns the speech APIs (recognizer, mic, TTS), and
host-page-adaptation owns the page the answer is typed into. Between them
sits extension/src/matching/ and extension/src/conversation/ — pure code
that imports no browser API and touches no DOM, and where the voice
interface is actually won or lost. No canon pack mentions speech at all,
so this is a third facet with no home.

Distilled only from how this project really works: the command lexicon
and its live-reported mishearings (commands.js), the two normalizations
and crossword number conventions (normalize.js), n-best expansion with
provenance and explicit caps (evaluate.js), semantic SAY payloads
(machine.js) rendered in one English module (phrases.js), and the
REQ-ANS/CMD/READ/SPCH requirement families.

One rule descends to a check: intent-phrases-unique — a phrase table
walked as a lexicon must not list the same surface phrase under two
intents, since both consumption shapes (inverted lookup, arm-by-arm
match) resolve that by table position and the losing intent silently
becomes unreachable. It judges only tables actually walked as a lexicon
(a synonym map read by key legitimately repeats values) and scopes
duplicates per arm. Red-first fixtures cover both violating shapes, the
quiet shapes, the naive alternative wrongly firing on them, and this
repo's real extension/src tree — asserting first that the tree really
does ship three walked lexicons for the rule to reach.

Everything else lands as RULES.md prose, and the pack is declared as
local/voice-dialog in .claudinite-checks.json so it activates.

{"sha":"e164c840b33339dc2e27b811a270cbebba9c5e19","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/CrosswordChat/commit/e164c840b33339dc2e27b811a270cbebba9c5e19","commit":{"message":"Claudinite growth: convert the interim-results rule to a check (#132)

Prose-to-checks sweep of .claudinite/local/packs. The endpointing section of
browser-speech/RULES.md carries an always-testable clause among its judgment:
interim results are the "still speaking" signal and are never delivered to the
caller. That constrains a static signature — a file that turns `interimResults`
on and wires `result` in the same breath, yet never reads `isFinal`, cannot tell
a hypothesis from a decision and hands its caller both.

New blocking check `stt-interim-results-gated`, registered in the pack manifest,
with red-first fixtures: three violating sources (property wiring, an
addEventListener/TypeScript recognizer, an options bag) and six quiet ones
(isFinal branching, the legacy `.final` spelling, an explicit disable, an
`=== true` comparison, a configure-only file that wires no handler, and a
comment-only mention), plus this repo's real extension/src, which stays clean.
Both failure directions were proven: neutering the rule reds the firing
fixtures, dropping the isFinal guard reds the quiet ones and extension/src.

Deletion test applied to the endpointing paragraph: it stays whole. The check
covers only the interim/final distinction, while the paragraph also carries the
pause monitor itself and the measured 1.8 s window, which no check enforces —
so it is marked with the check pointer rather than trimmed, in the pack's
existing style. README check table and counts updated.

{"sha":"7ccc4f826422416338b67c116503864412bbcff9","html_url":"https://github.com/missingbulb/CrosswordChat/commit/7ccc4f826422416338b67c116503864412bbcff9","commit":{"message":"Claudinite: convert the dispatch-target rule to a check (#160)

Prose-to-checks sweep over `.claudinite/local/packs`. One conversion, in
`local/host-page-adaptation`.

The rule: "aim your events at a node inside the app's own subtree — a modern
app delegates key handling near its root, which is a descendant of <body>, so
an event dispatched at `document` or `body` bubbles past it and is never seen"
(RULES.md, "Never trust a write — verify by re-reading"). Always-testable: the
receiver at a `dispatchEvent` site is a static signature, and no existing check
looked at it — the sibling `synthetic-input-events-bubble` judges whether the
event *can* travel, never where it is aimed. Both can be satisfied and the
write still fail.

New check `input-events-target-app-subtree` (blocking): fires when a real-input
event (lib.mjs INPUT_EVENT_CLASSES, one constructor-alias hop and one
local-variable hop, exactly as the sibling resolves it) is dispatched at a
receiver written out literally as `document`, `document.body`,
`document.documentElement`, `window`/`globalThis`/`self`. A target the code
*resolves* — the `activeElement ?? cell ?? body` ladder a real adapter uses —
is beyond a static read and stays silent, which is why the repo's own
`writer.js` is quiet: the mistake is aiming at a global, not falling back to
one. CustomEvent and non-input events are never judged.

Red-first fixtures in pack.test.mjs: five firing cases (document, body,
documentElement/window/qualified, the variable hop, the aliased `fire()`
helper), six quiet ones (app node, resolved-target ladder, CustomEvent at
window, `new Event('resize')`, an unreadable local, a comment, test
scaffolding), the naive-grep case that shows the parsing is necessary, and the
corpus case over the real `extension/src/`. Neutering the rule's `run` fails
exactly the five firing tests — see-it-fail, verified.

`assignedTo` moves from synthetic-input-events-bubble.mjs into lib.mjs, since
both dispatch-site rules now resolve the same variable hop.

Deletion test on the prose: the paragraph STAYS WHOLE. It carries a second
rule the check does not cover (poll the re-read; the host renders
asynchronously) and the value the check cannot judge (which node to aim at
instead). Per the skill, prose is deleted whole or not at all — never trimmed
— so it keeps its text and gains a pointer to the check for the half now
mechanized, in the pack's established style.

{"number":166,"title":"Claudinite growth: discover local pack voice-dialog","body":"Refs #159 — weekly `growth-discover-packs` run.

## The gap

Manifesting the repo's stack and holding it against the mounted canon shelf and the two existing local packs left exactly one unhomed facet: **the language layer of the spoken interface**.

- `browser-speech` (local) owns the speech **APIs** — recognizer lifecycle, mic capture and constraints, TTS delivery, endpointing, error taxonomy. Its own charter: "every rule judges a browser API contract".
- `host-page-adaptation` (local) owns the **page** the resolved answer is typed into.
- Between them sits `extension/src/matching/` + `extension/src/conversation/` — pure code that imports no browser API and touches no DOM: the lexicon, normalization, n-best candidate evaluation, ambiguity handling, the state machine's semantic payloads, and the clue verbalizer. No canon pack mentions speech at all, and neither sibling local pack owns it.

Everything else in the manifest was already homed and is **not** re-created here: MV3 build/runtime → canon `chrome-extension`; release/store/privacy-page → canon `chrome-extension-release`; scheduled workflows → `github-actions`; the requirements trace + satori/resvg/pixelmatch visual goldens → canon `spec-driven-product` + `executable-requirements` (both already declared); the NYT DOM and the fake-host fixture → local `host-page-adaptation`.

## What's in the pack

`.claudinite/local/packs/voice-dialog/`, declared as `local/voice-dialog` in `.claudinite-checks.json`.

**One check** (the only rule with an honest deterministic signature):

| Check | Enforces | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| `intent-phrases-unique` | no surface phrase under two intents | blocking |

A phrase table is either **inverted** into a phrase-keyed lookup (`EXACT.set(phrase, intent)`) or **matched arm by arm** (`phrases.includes(norm)`). Both resolve a phrase listed under two intents by table *position* — last writer wins, or first arm wins — so the losing intent becomes unreachable through that wording with no symptom at the site of the mistake. These tables grow by accretion (every live mishearing gets appended to the arm it was heard for: this repo's `undue`, `a cross`, bare `anyway`), so the collision arrives long after both arms were written.

Precision, because a false alarm here is worse than the bug:
- judges only tables actually **walked as a lexicon** — a synonym/expansion map read by key legitimately repeats its values (this repo's homophone lookup names every word of a set under every word of it);
- scopes duplicates **per arm** — the same phrase twice in one arm is redundancy, not ambiguity;
- skips arms holding anything but string literals; strips comments first.

**Everything else lands as `RULES.md` prose** (nine sections), each grounded in a named file/requirement: the lexicon as a record of what the recognizer actually emits; the escape hatch out of the command namespace; normalize-once; use the n-best and keep provenance (with the three explicit expansion caps); never resolve an ambiguity by picking; the utterance shapes humans really speak in; say the least that resolves the turn; keep the policy language-free and the language in one file; speak what the eye would have seen.

Nothing is invented — the README lists the provenance file by file.

## Green

- `npm test` → 452 passed (22 files), including the 14 red-first cases in `pack.test.mjs`.
- `npm run trace` → 111/111 Active requirements covered, no phantom IDs.
- Red-first proves it in two directions: the violating fixtures fire (both consumption shapes), the quiet fixtures stay quiet, and those same quiet fixtures are confirmed to **wrongly fire** against the naive alternative the parsing exists to avoid. The repo-corpus case asserts *first* that `extension/src` really does ship three walked lexicons (`PHRASES`, `CHOICE_PHRASES`, `CONTROLS`) for the rule to reach, and only then that it is silent on them — so it cannot pass vacuously.

## Reviewer's eye

A new pack's checks reach every session and every CI run in this repo the moment it merges, so **auto-merge is deliberately not armed**. The judgement calls worth a second opinion: whether `intent-phrases-unique`'s "walked as a lexicon" gate is the right precision boundary, and whether the pack's territory line against `browser-speech` reads correctly to you.

{"number":165,"title":"Claudinite: convert the dispatch-target rule to a check (#160)","body":"Weekly **prose-to-checks** sweep over `.claudinite/local/packs` (tracking issue #160). One conversion, in `local/host-page-adaptation`. Nothing under `.claudinite/shared/` was touched.

## The rule converted

From `host-page-adaptation/RULES.md`, "Never trust a write — verify by re-reading":

> …aim your events at a node **inside the app's own subtree** — the selected element if it has focus, otherwise a known app node. A modern app delegates key handling near its root, which is a descendant of ``, so an event dispatched at `document` or `body` bubbles *past* it and is never seen.

It clears the skill's first gate (it governs how we drive a host page, not what this product renders), it is always-testable (the receiver at a `dispatchEvent` site is a static signature), and no existing check covered it: the sibling `synthetic-input-events-bubble` judges whether the event **can** travel, never **where** it is aimed. Both can be satisfied and the write still fail — `document.dispatchEvent(new KeyboardEvent('keydown', { bubbles: true }))` bubbles perfectly, past nothing.

## The check

`input-events-target-app-subtree`, **blocking**, in `local/host-page-adaptation`.

Fires when a real-input event (the `INPUT_EVENT_CLASSES` set, resolved through one constructor-alias hop and one local-variable hop, exactly as the sibling resolves it) is dispatched at a receiver written out **literally** as `document`, `document.body`, `document.documentElement`, or `window`/`globalThis`/`self` (optionally qualified, e.g. `window.document.body`).

Parsed, not grepped, and quiet in the deliberate direction:

- a target the code **resolves** — the `activeElement ?? cell ?? body` ladder a real adapter picks with — is beyond a static read, so the rule says nothing. That is why this repo's own `page-adapter/writer.js` is quiet: the mistake the rule is after is *aiming* at a global, not *falling back* to one.
- `CustomEvent` (your own signal to your own listener) and non-input events (`new Event('resize')`, which is exactly what `window` is the right target for) are never judged.
- comments are stripped first, so prose describing the trap cannot fire it.

## See-it-fail

Red-first fixtures in `pack.test.mjs`: five firing cases (`document`, `document.body`, documentElement/window/qualified, the variable hop, the aliased `fire()` helper), six quiet ones (app node, resolved-target ladder, `CustomEvent` at window, `new Event('resize')`, an unreadable local, a comment, test scaffolding), the naive-grep case proving the parsing is *necessary*, and the corpus case over the real `extension/src/`.

Neutering the rule's `run` to return `[]` fails **exactly** the five firing tests and nothing else — verified, then reverted.

## Deletion test — the prose stays whole

Applied to the paragraph the check now stands beside: it **stays**, untrimmed. It carries a second rule the check does not cover (poll the re-read — the host renders asynchronously, so the DOM right after your event is the DOM *before* the app processed it) and the value the check cannot judge (which node to aim at *instead*). Per the skill, prose is deleted whole or not at all — never trimmed — so the paragraph keeps its text and gains a pointer to the check for the half now mechanized, in the pack's established style. `README.md`'s check table and enforcement column are updated to match.

## Also in the diff

`assignedTo` moves from `synthetic-input-events-bubble.mjs` into `lib.mjs` — both dispatch-site rules now resolve the same one-variable hop, and the existing fixtures cover that path.

## Green

[Resource from github at repo://missingbulb/crosswordchat/sha/f73bb6fd08fc9bfe7108563d45ec274eae705150/contents/.claudinite/local/packs/host-page-adaptation/RULES.md] # Adapting to a host page — the judgment core

Working inside a web app you do not own: reading its DOM, driving it with synthetic input,
watching it change, and putting your own UI into its chrome. The mechanical rules — that a
page observer is disconnected, that a synthetic input event bubbles — are this pack's two
checks; what follows is only what no check can decide for you.

Each rule below is a judgment about being a guest in someone else's page, and holds for any
code that does it — a userscript, an automation layer, an extension's content script. Where
one cites this repo — a file, a requirement id, a date — that is the **evidence** it was drawn
from, not the scope it applies to.

The premise underneath all of it: **the host will change its markup without telling you, and
your code will not throw when it does.** A selector that matches nothing returns null; a click
on a renamed button never happens. Every rule here is about making that failure loud, local,
and cheap to fix.

## Quarantine the host's DOM knowledge in one module

All of it, behind an interface expressed in your own vocabulary — here `page-adapter/` returns
a `Snapshot` and takes `enterAnswer`, and the crossword model, the dialog policy and the
matcher never learn that the page exists (REQ-PAGE-011, `dev/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` §2). Two
things follow, and both are worth the discipline:

- A redesign is a **one-directory** change, and the blast radius is knowable before you start.
- The rest of the codebase becomes testable without a browser at all — the pure layers here
  (`puzzle-model/`, `matching/`, `conversation/`) are pure *because* the quarantine holds.

Inside that module, put **every selector and class string in one file**, and change values only
there (`page-adapter/selectors.js`). A selector inlined at its use site is the one that gets
missed when the host renames a class.

Enforce the quarantine mechanically, by token: the repo's arch test fails if the host's class
prefix (`xwd__`) appears in code outside `page-adapter/`.

## Identify host UI by a net, not by a selector

A single selector is a bet that one class name survives. Cast a net instead, and make the last
strand semantic:

- class nets that accept a family (`[class*="xwd__toolbar"]`), not one exact name;
- attribute and role hooks the host is less likely to churn (`role="cell"`, `data-testid`,
  `aria-label`);
- and a **text/shape fallback** underneath: the splash is found by class net *or* by "a visible
  container whose text says 'Ready to start solving' with a Play-ish button in it, whatever its
  classes are called" (`page-adapter/splash.js`); the pause veil is found by its copy plus
  visibility (`reader.js isPaused`).

Visibility is part of identity. Hosts keep dismissed modals in the DOM, so a match that ignores
`display`/`visibility`/zero-size will keep reporting a splash you already cleared.

## Write down what you verified the selectors against, and when

The selectors file is the only place in the codebase whose truth lives on someone else's
server, so it carries its own provenance: the date and page it was last verified against, the
captured markup it was read from, and — most valuable — the **negative** findings.
`selectors.js` records that the state classes sit on the `<rect>` and not the `<g>`, that the
pencil button exposes no `aria-pressed` and no class change, that the letter/number `<text>`
nodes carry no distinguishing classes and the class-based selectors match nothing live. Each of
those is an hour of somebody's life, and none of it is recoverable from the code.

## Ship a probe, and make a broken page a finding rather than an exception

One entry point that reports the health of every selector against the live page —
`page-adapter/probe.js`, REQ-PAGE-009, run from the in-page menu (MT-01). It is the first thing
to run when a user says "it stopped working", and it turns "the extension is broken" into "the
clue-list wrapper selector matches 0, want 2".

It must **never throw**: a probe that dies on the first missing element reports one fault and
hides the other nine. Collect a row per selector and return them all — and have it capture
forensics for the things you could *not* read (the probe here dumps the pencil button's
attributes precisely because its ON state has never been readable), so the next report arrives
with the evidence already in it.

## Mirror the host in a fixture, and let the fixture define the expected shape

A saved, simplified copy of the host page (`extension-test/fixtures/fake-nyt/`, served by
`npm run fixture`) mirrors the selectors exactly, and the integration tests drive that. It buys
two things a live page cannot: the read/write/watch cycle is testable in CI at all, and the
whole voice loop is rehearsable locally without a subscription (`npm run build:dev` widens the
matches to `localhost:8787`, MT-23).

Its limit is the same as its virtue — **the fixture only ever shows you the markup you already
knew about**, so a passing suite is never evidence about the live page. Keep a manual-test
document for what only the real host can answer (`dev/docs/MANUAL-TESTS.md`), and treat every
live finding as a fixture update.

## Never trust a write — verify by re-reading

Address the target by position rather than relying on the host's own cursor conventions (click
each cell, then type one letter — immune to the host's advance-on-type and skip-filled
settings), then **read the DOM back and confirm what you meant is there** (REQ-PAGE-007). The
host may ignore untrusted events, may auto-advance differently than you assumed, may reject the
input silently; the re-read is the only thing that distinguishes those from success.

Poll the re-read, don't do it synchronously after the last dispatch: the host renders
asynchronously (React here), so the DOM immediately after your event is the DOM *before* the
app processed it. And aim your events at a node **inside the app's own subtree** — the selected
element if it has focus, otherwise a known app node. A modern app delegates key handling near
its root, which is a descendant of `<body>`, so an event dispatched at `document` or `body`
bubbles *past* it and is never seen (`page-adapter/writer.js`).

## A synthetic keystroke must carry the fields a real one would

The browser fills in the deprecated `keyCode`/`which`/`charCode` on every real keystroke; on
a synthetic one they are plain init fields that default to 0, so
`new KeyboardEvent('keydown', { key: 'A' })` reaches the page as a keystroke whose keyCode is
0. Deprecated is not the same as unread: hosts with a long-lived key-handling layer still
branch on the legacy fields — this one does (verified live, MT-02) — and a 0 matches nothing,
so the handler runs and nothing happens, indistinguishable from "the app ignores untrusted
events". Mirror the real event instead: `keyCode` and `which` alongside `key`/`code`,
`charCode` on `keypress`, and the full keydown → keypress → keyup sequence a real keystroke
produces (`page-adapter/writer.js` `keyEventInit`/`typeKey`).

Build the init in **one helper** and spread it at the single dispatch site, so fidelity is one
function's job. That factoring is also why this rule is prose rather than a check: the init a
well-factored adapter dispatches is opaque to a static scan (`{ ...init }` could carry
anything), so a check here could only ever police code that bypasses the helper — and the
mistake in that code is bypassing the helper, not the field it then forgot.

## Put back any host state you borrowed, and degrade when you cannot read it

Driving a host toggle means driving it back: pencil mode is set to match the write and restored
afterwards, so the user's own typing mode is never stolen (REQ-PAGE-012).

You will often be unable to read the state you are toggling — the live pencil button has no
`aria-pressed` and no class change, so "on or off?" is genuinely unanswerable. Design for the
unreadable case as the **normal** one, not the error case: fall back to click parity, and let
the feature that depends on it degrade (the letters still land; only the pencil softening is
lost, REQ-ANS-019) rather than failing the operation.

## The host has a lifecycle of its own, and its blank states are not your user's doing

You are sharing the page with an app that has its own timers, veils and modals, and each one
looks like something else from inside your adapter:

- **Idle timers.** This host auto-pauses a quiet puzzle after ~30 s of no keyboard input. A
  voice solver touches no keyboard, so the adapter sends a bare `Shift` keydown/keyup on every
  heard command — a real key event that types nothing and moves nothing (REQ-LIFE-017). Choose
  the nudge so it cannot mutate state, and drive it from real user activity, never from a timer
  of your own: when the user really has gone quiet, the host *should* pause and your session
  should end with it.
- **Veils that blank the content.** The pause veil empties the visible entries. A change watcher
  that diffs first and checks for the veil second will read that as the user clearing the whole
  grid. Check for the host's own overlay states **before** diffing, report the state once, and
  return (`page-adapter/watcher.js`).
- **Pre-content splashes.** The board may not exist for minutes while a "Ready to start
  solving?" modal is up. Absence of the content is not absence of the app.

## Be inert when you are off

Your code loads on the host's page whether or not the user is using you, so **doing nothing is
the resting state** (REQ-NFR-004). Watchers are created on demand and stopped with the session;
nothing polls; nothing observes between sessions.

Keep load-time page changes to an explicit, minimal carve-out — here exactly one: mounting the
toolbar button (REQ-LIFE-012). Mount it by waiting with a `MutationObserver` that **disconnects
the moment the element lands** (the `page-observers-disconnected` check), and give up only when
the host shows no app markup at all — a slow render or a splash must not cost you the button,
but an archive page must not leave you waiting forever.

1	// The one SessionEnd command a consumer's .claude/settings.json wires. Like its
2	// siblings the address is the stable contract (#385: the settings file changes as
3	// seldom as possible), and like the SessionStart orchestrator it is a RUNNER, not a
4	// step: it invokes each ACTIVE pack's own `session-end.mjs`, discovered structurally
5	// exactly as tasks, prose and skills are. Core never names the pack whose step it
6	// runs, and never learns what one does — a session-end step is pack content, and the
7	// engine's whole part is "invoke it, once, when the session ends"
8	// (skill-usage-metrics DESIGN §3.3).
9	//
10	// SessionEnd, not Stop. Stop fires at every turn end (and already runs the
11	// conformance checks); a step that writes anything per-session would fire once per
12	// TURN there. SessionEnd fires once, when the session ends.
13	//
14	// BEST EFFORT AS A HOOK, and that is enough there: a container reclaimed by timeout
15	// never fires it, so nothing may depend on it having run — every firing strictly
16	// enriches the record, every miss leaves exactly the prior behaviour.
17	//
18	// AND EXPLICITLY INVOCABLE, which is what makes unattended sessions countable at
19	// all. An UNATTENDED session — the scheduler's executor, running a dispatch in a
20	// cloud container nobody is sitting in front of — ends when its container is
21	// reclaimed, so the hook is exactly the firing that does not happen, and every one
22	// of those sessions used to leave no record anywhere. So the executor runs this
23	// runner itself as its last step (engine/scheduler/executor.md), naming the dispatch
24	// issue in `CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ISSUE`. Steps must therefore tolerate being run
25	// mid-session: the transcript is complete only up to the invocation, and the later
26	// hook firing (when it happens at all) is a second event over the same session,
27	// which the capture step's session-keyed delta already makes safe.
28	//
29	// FAIL-SOFT, absolutely. A session must never fail to end because of this hook, so
30	// every error — a step that throws, a step that hangs, a broken pack registry — is
31	// swallowed, recorded via hooklog, and exited 0. The per-step bound is a hard kill;
32	// nothing here can wedge a session.
33	import { spawnSync } from 'node:child_process';
34	import { existsSync, readFileSync } from 'node:fs';
35	import { join, dirname } from 'node:path';
36	import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';
37	import { hooklog } from '../checks/helpers/hook-log.mjs';
38	
39	// The step file an active pack contributes, if it ships one.
40	export const STEP_FILE = 'session-end.mjs';
